19	### A topological lemma
20	
21	Suppose
22	\[
23	F:S^a\times S^b\longrightarrow
24	\mathbb R^J\oplus\mathbb R^J\oplus\mathbb R^J
25	\]
26	is continuous, and write \(F=(F_1,F_2,F_{12})\). Suppose that replacing the first sphere coordinate by its antipode changes the signs of \(F_1,F_{12}\), and replacing the second coordinate by its antipode changes the signs of \(F_2,F_{12}\).

29	\[
30	x^Jy^J(x+y)^J\ne0
31	\quad\text{in}\quad
32	\mathbb F_2[x,y]/(x^{a+1},y^{b+1}),
33	\tag{1}
34	\]

37	Here is the vector-bundle proof. On
38	\[
39	B=\mathbb {RP}^{a}\times\mathbb {RP}^{b},
40	\]
41	let \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\) be the two tautological line bundles. The equivariance of \(F\) makes it a section of
42	\[
43	E=\lambda_1^{\oplus J}\oplus
44	\lambda_2^{\oplus J}\oplus
45	(\lambda_1\otimes\lambda_2)^{\oplus J}.
46	\]
47	The mod-two cohomology ring of \(B\) is the ring in (1), with
48	\(x=w_1(\lambda_1)\) and \(y=w_1(\lambda_2)\). Thus the Whitney product formula gives
49	\[
50	w_{3J}(E)=x^Jy^J(x+y)^J.
51	\]
52	A nowhere-zero section would split off a trivial line bundle and force this top Stiefel–Whitney class to vanish. This proves the lemma.

54	### Applying the lemma to measures

56	Let
57	\[
58	J=2n-1,\qquad D=3n-1.
59	\]
60	We claim that every \(J\) absolutely continuous probability measures on \(\mathbb R^D\) admit an equipartition by two hyperplanes.
61	
62	Parameterize an oriented hyperplane through the origin by \(v\in S^{D-1}\), using
63	\[
64	h_v(z)=v\cdot z,
65	\]
66	and parameterize an oriented affine hyperplane by \(w=(u,t)\in S^D\), using
67	\[
68	h_w(z)=u\cdot z+t.
69	\]
70	The parameters with \(u=0\) represent constant signs; they will not occur at a zero of the test map.
71	
72	For each measure \(\mu_i\), define
73	\[
74	\begin{aligned}
75	A_i(v)&=\int \operatorname{sgn}(h_v(z))\,d\mu_i(z),\\
76	B_i(w)&=\int \operatorname{sgn}(h_w(z))\,d\mu_i(z),\\
77	C_i(v,w)&=\int \operatorname{sgn}(h_v(z))
78	                    \operatorname{sgn}(h_w(z))\,d\mu_i(z).
79	\end{aligned}
80	\]
81	These functions are continuous by dominated convergence and absolute continuity. They have precisely the equivariance required by the lemma.
82	
83	At a simultaneous zero, the measure of the region with signs
84	\((\varepsilon,\eta)\in\{-1,1\}^2\) is
85	\[
86	\frac14\bigl(1+\varepsilon A_i+\eta B_i+\varepsilon\eta C_i\bigr)
87	=\frac14.
88	\tag{2}
89	\]
90	
91	Take \(a=D-1\) and \(b=D\). We have
92	\[
93	a+b=3J.
94	\]
95	Consequently, the class in (1) is nonzero exactly when the coefficient of
96	\(x^{D-1}y^D\) is odd. That coefficient is
97	\[
98	\binom{J}{D-1-J}
99	=\binom{2n-1}{n-1}.
100	\]
101	Because \(2n=2^s\), in characteristic two
102	\[
103	(1+t)^{2n-1}=1+t+\cdots+t^{2n-1}.
104	\]
105	In particular, this binomial coefficient is odd. The topological lemma and (2) prove the claim.
106	
107	### Reducing both the number of measures and the dimension by one
108	
109	We now deduce that \(J-1\) measures can be equipartitioned in \(\mathbb R^{D-1}\).
110	
111	Let \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_{J-1}\) be the given measures. Regard \(\mathbb R^{D-1}\) as
112	\[
113	H=\mathbb R^{D-1}\times\{0\}\subset\mathbb R^D.
114	\]
115	For \(\epsilon>0\), replace each measure by the absolutely continuous product
116	\[
117	\mu_i\otimes N(0,\epsilon^2).
118	\]
119	Add one more measure: the standard Gaussian centered at
120	\[
121	p=(0,\ldots,0,1).
122	\]
123	The preceding result supplies two equipartitioning hyperplanes.
124	
125	Every bisector of the added Gaussian passes through \(p\). Normalize the affine coefficients of both hyperplanes to have Euclidean norm one and take a convergent subsequence as \(\epsilon\to0\). Both limiting hyperplanes still pass through \(p\).
126	
127	Neither limiting affine equation can vanish identically on \(H\): a hyperplane containing both \(H\) and \(p\notin H\) would be all of \(\mathbb R^D\).

132	\]

134	
135	Thus the limiting hyperplanes restrict to the required equipartition in \(H\). We have proved
136	\[
137	D_s\le D-1=3n-2.
138	\tag{3}
139	\]
140	
141	The four sign regions have positive measure, so they are all nonempty. Being intersections of open halfspaces, they are connected. Thus the complement has exactly four connected components, as required.

143	## 2. A definite nonsingular bilinear system
144	
145	The lower bound rests on the following explicit linear-algebra construction.
146	
147	### Lemma
148	
149	For every even \(n\ge4\), there exist \(2n-2\) real symmetric positive-definite \(n\times n\) matrices
150	\[
151	A_0,\ldots,A_{2n-3}
152	\]
153	such that
154	\[
155	x^TA_i y=0\quad\text{for every }i
156	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=0\ \text{or}\ y=0.
157	\tag{4}
158	\]
159	
160	### Proof
161	
162	Write \(n=2k\), where \(k\ge2\), and put
163	\[
164	L=2k-2=n-2.
165	\]
166	Identify \(\mathbb R^n\) with the complex polynomials of degree at most \(k-1\), by their coefficient vectors. Define
167	\[
168	p(t)=\prod_{\ell=0}^{L-1}(t-2^\ell).
169	\]
170	
171	For two coefficient vectors \(z,w\in\mathbb C^k\), let \(R(z,w)\in\mathbb C^L\) be the coefficient vector of
172	\[
173	z(t)w(t)\pmod {p(t)}.
174	\]
175	Also define the real bilinear forms
176	\[
177	\begin{aligned}
178	U(z,w)&=\operatorname{Re}\sum_{r=0}^{k-1}\overline{z_r}w_r,\\
179	V(z,w)&=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(
180	 i(\overline{z_0}w_1-\overline{z_1}w_0)\right).
181	\end{aligned}
182	\]
183	All the real coordinates of
184	\[
185	\mathcal B(z,w)=\bigl(U(z,w),V(z,w),
186	                         \operatorname{Re}R(z,w),\operatorname{Im}R(z,w)\bigr)
187	\tag{5}
188	\]
189	are symmetric real bilinear forms. There are
190	\[
191	2+2L=2n-2
192	\]
193	of them, and \(U\) is the ordinary real inner product.
194	
195	We show that (5) cannot vanish when both \(z\) and \(w\) are nonzero.
196	
197	If \(R(z,w)=0\), then
198	\[
199	z(t)w(t)=c\,p(t),\qquad c\ne0.
200	\]
201	Both factors must have degree \(k-1\). Since the roots of \(p\) are distinct and real, we can write
202	\[
203	z=\alpha f,\qquad w=\beta g,
204	\]
205	where \(f,g\) are monic real polynomials whose root sets partition the roots of \(p\), and \(\alpha,\beta\ne0\).
206	
207	Write
208	\[
209	a=\sum_{r=0}^{k-1}f_rg_r,\qquad
210	b=f_0g_1-f_1g_0.
211	\]
212	All coefficients of a monic polynomial of degree \(k-1\) with positive roots have alternating, nonzero signs. Hence
213	\[
214	f_rg_r>0\quad(0\le r<k),\qquad a>0.
215	\tag{6}
216	\]
217	
218	Let \(I\subset\{0,\ldots,L-1\}\) index the roots belonging to \(f\). Logarithmic differentiation at zero gives
219	\[
220	\frac{b}{p(0)}
221	=
222	\sum_{\ell\in I}2^{-\ell}
223	-\sum_{\ell\notin I}2^{-\ell}.
224	\tag{7}
225	\]
226	Multiplying the right side by \(2^{L-1}\) gives an odd integer: its last summand is \(1\) or \(-1\), and all other summands are even. Therefore
227	\[
228	b\ne0.
229	\tag{8}
230	\]
231	
232	Now
233	\[
234	U(z,w)=a\,\operatorname{Re}(\overline\alpha\beta),\qquad
235	V(z,w)=-b\,\operatorname{Im}(\overline\alpha\beta).
236	\]
237	By (6) and (8), both can vanish only if \(\overline\alpha\beta=0\), a contradiction. This proves nonsingularity of (5).
238	
239	Represent its coordinates by real symmetric matrices
240	\[
241	C_0=I_n,C_1,\ldots,C_{2n-3}.
242	\]
243	Set \(A_0=I_n\), and, for \(i\ge1\), choose
244	\[
245	\lambda_i=1+\max_r\sum_q |(C_i)_{rq}|,\qquad
246	A_i=C_i+\lambda_i I_n.
247	\]
248	Each \(A_i\) is positive definite, for instance by strict diagonal dominance.
249	
250	If all \(x^TA_i y\) vanish, the equation for \(A_0\) gives \(x^Ty=0\). The remaining equations then give \(x^TC_i y=0\) for every \(i\), contradicting nonsingularity unless \(x=0\) or \(y=0\). This proves the lemma. ∎
251	
252	## 3. The Gaussian counterexample in dimension \(3n-3\)
253	
254	Let \(j=2n-2\), and decompose
255	\[
256	\mathbb R^{3n-3}=\mathbb R^{j-1}\oplus\mathbb R^n.
257	\]
258	Choose \(j\) centers
259	\[
260	c_0=0,\qquad c_i=(e_i,0)\quad(1\le i\le j-1).
261	\]
262	Using the matrices from the lemma, let \(\mu_i\) be the Gaussian with mean \(c_i\) and covariance
263	\[
264	\Sigma_i=
265	\begin{pmatrix}
266	I_{j-1}&0\\
267	0&A_i
268	\end{pmatrix}.
269	\tag{9}
270	\]
271	These are nonsingular Gaussians, hence absolutely continuous Borel probability measures.
272	
273	Suppose two hyperplanes equipartition all these measures. Each hyperplane must individually bisect every \(\mu_i\).
274	
275	A hyperplane bisects a nonsingular Gaussian precisely when it contains its mean. Thus each of our hyperplanes contains every \(c_i\), and consequently has equation
276	\[
277	x\cdot z=0
278	\]
279	for a nonzero normal \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). Write \(x,y\) for the two normals.
280	
281	For the Gaussian \(\mu_i\), the two defining linear forms have covariance
282	\[
283	x^TA_i y.
284	\]
285	For a centered bivariate Gaussian with correlation \(\rho\),
286	\[
287	\Pr(X>0,Y>0)=\frac14+\frac{\arcsin\rho}{2\pi}.
288	\tag{10}
289	\]
290	This follows by expressing two independent standard normals in polar coordinates: the probability is the angle of the corresponding wedge divided by \(2\pi\).
291	
292	Consequently, four equal quadrant probabilities require \(\rho=0\). In our construction this means
293	\[
294	x^TA_i y=0\qquad(0\le i<j),
295	\]
296	contradicting the lemma.
297	
298	Therefore these \(j\) Gaussian measures have no such equipartition in dimension \(3n-3\).
299	
300	Finally, the universal equipartition property is monotone in the dimension: if it holds in dimension \(d\), project any measures in a larger dimension onto \(\mathbb R^d\), equipartition the projected measures, and lift the hyperplanes. The projected measures remain absolutely continuous by Fubini's theorem. Thus failure in dimension \(3n-3\) implies
301	\[
302	D_s\ge3n-2.
303	\tag{11}
304	\]
305	Together, (3) and (11) give the asserted answer.
306	
307	## 4. Exact Python checks
308	
309	The following code uses exact integer and symbolic arithmetic, not numerical searches. For each supplied \(s\), it:
310	
311	- constructs all the bilinear-form matrices;
312	- checks every matrix coefficient against the polynomial definition;
313	- certifies positive definiteness by strict diagonal dominance;
314	- exhaustively checks every possible complementary root factorization;
315	- checks the odd-integer identity in (7);
316	- checks the Euler-class parity and all dimension identities.
317	
318	The general proof above avoids any need to enumerate infinitely many values of \(s\). The code checks the finite algebraic certificates for each requested value.

330	        for j, y in enumerate(b):
331	            out[i + j] += x * y

141	## 2. A definite nonsingular bilinear system
142	
143	The lower bound rests on the following explicit linear-algebra construction.
144	
145	### Lemma
146	
147	For every even \(n\ge4\), there exist \(2n-2\) real symmetric positive-definite \(n\times n\) matrices
148	\[
149	A_0,\ldots,A_{2n-3}
150	\]
151	such that
152	\[
153	x^TA_i y=0\quad\text{for every }i
154	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=0\ \text{or}\ y=0.
155	\tag{4}
156	\]
157	
158	### Proof
159	
160	Write \(n=2k\), where \(k\ge2\), and put
161	\[
162	L=2k-2=n-2.
163	\]
164	Identify \(\mathbb R^n\) with the complex polynomials of degree at most \(k-1\), by their coefficient vectors. Define
165	\[
166	p(t)=\prod_{\ell=0}^{L-1}(t-2^\ell).
167	\]
168	
169	For two coefficient vectors \(z,w\in\mathbb C^k\), let \(R(z,w)\in\mathbb C^L\) be the coefficient vector of
170	\[
171	z(t)w(t)\pmod {p(t)}.
172	\]
173	Also define the real bilinear forms
174	\[
175	\begin{aligned}
176	U(z,w)&=\operatorname{Re}\sum_{r=0}^{k-1}\overline{z_r}w_r,\\
177	V(z,w)&=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(
178	 i(\overline{z_0}w_1-\overline{z_1}w_0)\right).
179	\end{aligned}
180	\]
181	All the real coordinates of
182	\[
183	\mathcal B(z,w)=\bigl(U(z,w),V(z,w),
184	                         \operatorname{Re}R(z,w),\operatorname{Im}R(z,w)\bigr)
185	\tag{5}
186	\]
187	are symmetric real bilinear forms. There are
188	\[
189	2+2L=2n-2
190	\]
191	of them, and \(U\) is the ordinary real inner product.
192	
193	We show that (5) cannot vanish when both \(z\) and \(w\) are nonzero.
194	
195	If \(R(z,w)=0\), then
196	\[
197	z(t)w(t)=c\,p(t),\qquad c\ne0.
198	\]
199	Both factors must have degree \(k-1\). Since the roots of \(p\) are distinct and real, we can write
200	\[
201	z=\alpha f,\qquad w=\beta g,
202	\]
203	where \(f,g\) are monic real polynomials whose root sets partition the roots of \(p\), and \(\alpha,\beta\ne0\).
204	
205	Write
206	\[
207	a=\sum_{r=0}^{k-1}f_rg_r,\qquad
208	b=f_0g_1-f_1g_0.
209	\]
210	All coefficients of a monic polynomial of degree \(k-1\) with positive roots have alternating, nonzero signs. Hence
211	\[
212	f_rg_r>0\quad(0\le r<k),\qquad a>0.
213	\tag{6}
214	\]
215	
216	Let \(I\subset\{0,\ldots,L-1\}\) index the roots belonging to \(f\). Logarithmic differentiation at zero gives
217	\[
218	\frac{b}{p(0)}
219	=
220	\sum_{\ell\in I}2^{-\ell}
221	-\sum_{\ell\notin I}2^{-\ell}.
222	\tag{7}
223	\]
224	Multiplying the right side by \(2^{L-1}\) gives an odd integer: its last summand is \(1\) or \(-1\), and all other summands are even. Therefore
225	\[
226	b\ne0.
227	\tag{8}
228	\]
229	
230	Now
231	\[
232	U(z,w)=a\,\operatorname{Re}(\overline\alpha\beta),\qquad
233	V(z,w)=-b\,\operatorname{Im}(\overline\alpha\beta).
234	\]
235	By (6) and (8), both can vanish only if \(\overline\alpha\beta=0\), a contradiction. This proves nonsingularity of (5).
236	
237	Represent its coordinates by real symmetric matrices
238	\[
239	C_0=I_n,C_1,\ldots,C_{2n-3}.
240	\]
241	Set \(A_0=I_n\), and, for \(i\ge1\), choose
242	\[
243	\lambda_i=1+\max_r\sum_q |(C_i)_{rq}|,\qquad
244	A_i=C_i+\lambda_i I_n.
245	\]
246	Each \(A_i\) is positive definite, for instance by strict diagonal dominance.
247	
248	If all \(x^TA_i y\) vanish, the equation for \(A_0\) gives \(x^Ty=0\). The remaining equations then give \(x^TC_i y=0\) for every \(i\), contradicting nonsingularity unless \(x=0\) or \(y=0\). This proves the lemma. ∎

250	## 3. The Gaussian counterexample in dimension \(3n-3\)
251	
252	Let \(j=2n-2\), and decompose
253	\[
254	\mathbb R^{3n-3}=\mathbb R^{j-1}\oplus\mathbb R^n.
255	\]
256	Choose \(j\) centers
257	\[
258	c_0=0,\qquad c_i=(e_i,0)\quad(1\le i\le j-1).
259	\]
260	Using the matrices from the lemma, let \(\mu_i\) be the Gaussian with mean \(c_i\) and covariance
261	\[
262	\Sigma_i=
263	\begin{pmatrix}
264	I_{j-1}&0\\
265	0&A_i
266	\end{pmatrix}.
267	\tag{9}
268	\]
269	These are nonsingular Gaussians, hence absolutely continuous Borel probability measures.
270	
271	Suppose two hyperplanes equipartition all these measures. Each hyperplane must individually bisect every \(\mu_i\).
272	
273	A hyperplane bisects a nonsingular Gaussian precisely when it contains its mean. Thus each of our hyperplanes contains every \(c_i\), and consequently has equation
274	\[
275	x\cdot z=0
276	\]
277	for a nonzero normal \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). Write \(x,y\) for the two normals.
278	
279	For the Gaussian \(\mu_i\), the two defining linear forms have covariance
280	\[
281	x^TA_i y.
282	\]
283	For a centered bivariate Gaussian with correlation \(\rho\),
284	\[
285	\Pr(X>0,Y>0)=\frac14+\frac{\arcsin\rho}{2\pi}.
286	\tag{10}
287	\]
288	This follows by expressing two independent standard normals in polar coordinates: the probability is the angle of the corresponding wedge divided by \(2\pi\).
289	
290	Consequently, four equal quadrant probabilities require \(\rho=0\). In our construction this means
291	\[
292	x^TA_i y=0\qquad(0\le i<j),
293	\]
294	contradicting the lemma.
295	
296	Therefore these \(j\) Gaussian measures have no such equipartition in dimension \(3n-3\).
297	
298	Finally, the universal equipartition property is monotone in the dimension: if it holds in dimension \(d\), project any measures in a larger dimension onto \(\mathbb R^d\), equipartition the projected measures, and lift the hyperplanes. The projected measures remain absolutely continuous by Fubini's theorem. Thus failure in dimension \(3n-3\) implies
299	\[
300	D_s\ge3n-2.
301	\tag{11}
302	\]
303	Together, (3) and (11) give the asserted answer.
